rv.q: It’s the perfect, bittersweet snapshot of our age and Wynne has much to say about the internet, with all its perils – and also possibilities.
Cuckoo makes for a cheerful if aimless evening.
But in the end, the ambiguity also breaks it.
There are times, though, when the play, directed by Vicky Featherstone, wavers and is in danger of coming to a standstill.
Yet Wynne’s domestic affair finally feels too slight to sound the depths of our current malaise.
But I’ve no idea why this play has been put on.
Like a couple of hours lost to Twitter, this play passes the time, but leaves you questioning what, if anything, you really got out of it.
The play is as delicious as those fish and chips.
The family dynamic is wonderfully enchanting, the bittersweet chemistry palpable from the outset thanks to subtle but towering performances.
Cuckoo is alarming, to be sure, and highly entertaining too.
So, Michael Wynne’s rather lovely, if uneven, new play is perfectly named.
Unfortunately, it's at this point that the wheels come off slightly and the play founders.

Vicky Featherstone’s production has the realism of a Merseyside soap opera threaded with gentle humour and a hint that something unusual, even supernatural could happen, but it never does, though there is an enigmatic ending.
Instead, Wynne’s writing feels slack and underpowered, full of loose ends and flaccid observations.
A must-see, particularly for those who've not thought the Royal Court could rock with laughter.
Cuckoo catches the zeitgeist of the moment in a classically theatrical living room drama style.
This commentary on British society is clever and compelling but ultimately the amount of unanswered questions could leave you feeling a little dissatisfied.
It’s a fascinating new play, and one that I’m sure will be just as equally well-received by its audiences in Liverpool after the Royal Court run concludes.
I recommend going to watch it if you’re into dark humour and social commentary, although do read the trigger warnings provided on the Royal Court’s website in advance.

cn.t: Wynne's Scouse dark comedy about four generations of women earns warm laughs but divides critics—some praise its humane relatability and sharp dialogue, while others find it aimless and lacking substance beneath its sitcom surface.
